newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin aide rejects parliament's charges.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin aide rejects parliament's charges.

text.p: Russia's opposition-dominated parliament, which is already pressing Boris Yeltsin to quit on health grounds, agreed on Tuesday to debate a new request to the president to investigate his chief aide for corruption.
Anatoly Chubais, who as architect of Yeltsin's free market reforms and privatisations has long been a prime target for the communists, flatly denied the accusations.

Viktor Ilyukhin, the communist chairman of the State Duma security committee, told reporters the lower house's business managers had agreed in principle to debate on Friday a motion alleging that Chubais, the Kremlin chief-of-staff, might have broken laws barring officials from earning money privately.

Chubais told Interfax news agency: "I appreciate the attention paid to me by the Duma council. Unfortunately, I am forced to disappoint the respected deputies -- I paid taxes on my 1996 income in full, in line with Russian law."
"Incidentally, the sum I paid was 515 million roubles (about $100,000). I call on comrade Ilyukhin and his colleagues to follow my example -- pay your taxes and tell society about it."
Chubais said his main earnings were from lectures and consultations before he joined Yeltsin's staff after the president was re-elected in July. Chubais ran his campaign.
The Duma first urged Yeltsin to suspend the 41-year-old head of the Kremlin administration last year.

Ilyukhin, who was also behind a motion to be debated on Wednesday calling on the president to step down on health grounds, said the Duma had had no response to that first move against Chubais and the latest motion aimed to reinforce it.

Many of Yeltsin's opponents say his current pneumonia, coming so soon after a six-month absence for heart surgery, shows he is unfit to rule. They also complain Chubais has been running Russia in his absence as an unelected "regent".

The Duma's business managers will take a final decision on Thursday on whether Friday's plenary session should debate the motion that the house urge the president to investigate media allegations of financial impropriety by Chubais.
Ilyukhin distributed photocopies of what purported to be a credit card statement for an account belonging to Chubais.
Ilyukhin said they corroborated allegations that Chubais received significant payments in dollars after he was appointed to run the Kremlin administration in July.
In fact, the last major credit on the documents was in early August, which would not be inconsistent with Chubais's response that he earned the money before July.

"If A.B. Chubais actually received foreign currency funds for activity not linked to the fulfilment of his direct responsibilities as a civil servant, then this constitutes a crude violation of the Principles of State Service Act," the draft text of the address to the president read.
Arguing that this could mean Chubais had "taken bribes", it concluded: "It is essential to make a legal evaluation of all these facts and take steps according to current legislation."
